passages.title: Remembered faith and personal support answer shame about a chained teacher
passages.summary: The letter is addressed from Paul to Timothy, his beloved child. Paul remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him. He recalls the faith of Timothy’s grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. Timothy is to stir up God’s gift, given through Paul’s hands. God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control, not fear. Timothy should not be ashamed of the Lord or of Paul the prisoner. All in Asia turned away from Paul. Onesiphorus was not ashamed of his chain and searched for him in Rome.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Rome, Ephesus, and Corinth as city points where each is named.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches courage through power, love, and a sound mind. How does remembered family faith support courage before present danger?

contextNote.title: Remembered faith and personal support answer shame about a chained teacher
contextNote.text: Paul writes as a prisoner (verse 8), and many have left him (verse 15). Shame is the danger the chapter names three times. Verse 8 tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony or of Paul. Verse 12 says Paul is not ashamed, for he knows whom he trusted. Verse 16 praises Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of the chain. The ground for courage comes just before, in verse 7. God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control.

passages.title: Patient correction must accompany careful teaching and shared endurance
passages.summary: Timothy is to be strong in grace and pass the teaching to faithful people. He should endure hardship like a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer. Paul suffers in chains, but God’s word is not chained. A trustworthy saying follows: if we died with him, we will live with him. Timothy should avoid word fights and empty talk. Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened. A great house has vessels for honor and for dishonor. The Lord’s servant must be gentle and correct opponents with patience.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Rome, Ephesus, and Corinth as city points where each is named.

lds.text: Why must correction remain gentle when false teaching harms others?

contextNote.title: Patient correction must accompany careful teaching and shared endurance
contextNote.text: Verse 23 tells Timothy to refuse foolish questions, because they breed quarrels. Verse 24 gives the rule for the Lord’s servant: he must not quarrel. Three qualities replace quarreling: gentle toward all, able to teach, and patient. Verse 25 keeps correction in place but sets its tone: gentleness. The reason is hope for the opponent. God may give them repentance and knowledge of the truth. Verse 26 says they may yet escape the devil’s snare.

passages.title: Received Scripture equips conduct amid deceptive displays of religion
passages.summary: The letter warns that hard times will come in the last days. People will love themselves, money, and pleasure more than God. They will hold a form of godliness and deny its power. Such teachers resist the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. Timothy has followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, and sufferings at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. All who live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted. Timothy should continue in what he learned from childhood in the holy Scriptures. Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Rome, Ephesus, and Corinth as city points where each is named.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches that Scripture can make readers wise for salvation. How does Scripture's usefulness lead into good work rather than knowledge alone?

contextNote.title: Received Scripture equips conduct amid deceptive displays of religion
contextNote.text: Verse 13 says deceivers will grow worse. Verse 14 tells Timothy to stay with what he has learned. Verse 15 says the holy Scriptures can make him wise for salvation. Verse 16 lists four uses: teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. Verse 17 gives the purpose of all four. The person who belongs to God becomes complete. He is equipped “for every good work,” so the end of the list is action.

passages.title: Urgent teaching and ordinary needs stand together near the speaker's expected departure
passages.summary: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ, the judge of living and dead. Timothy is to announce the word and be ready at all times. A time will come when people gather teachers who please their ears. Paul says he is already being poured out. He has fought the good fight and kept the faith. He asks Timothy to come soon and bring Mark, a cloak, and the books. At his first defense no one stood with him, but the Lord did. He sends greetings and a blessing.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Rome, Ephesus, and Corinth as city points where each is named.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches continued faithfulness when hearers prefer false teaching. Why do ordinary requests remain beside confident language about completion and reward?

contextNote.title: Urgent teaching and ordinary needs stand together near the speaker's expected departure
contextNote.text: Verse 1 sets the charge before God and Christ the judge. Verse 2 gives five commands in a row. The first is to announce the word. The second is to be ready in season and out of season. Reprove, rebuke, and exhort follow, with patience and teaching. Verses 3–4 explain the urgency: hearers will turn from the truth to fables. Verse 6 adds another reason: Paul’s own departure is near.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: 2 Timothy: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Remembered faith and personal support answer shame about a chained teacher
steps.text: Paul writes as a prisoner (verse 8), and many have left him (verse 15). Shame is the danger the chapter names three times. Verse 8 tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony or of Paul. Verse 12 says Paul is not ashamed, for he knows whom he trusted. Verse 16 praises Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of the chain. The ground for courage comes just before, in verse 7. God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control.

steps.title: Patient correction must accompany careful teaching and shared endurance
steps.text: Verse 23 tells Timothy to refuse foolish questions, because they breed quarrels. Verse 24 gives the rule for the Lord’s servant: he must not quarrel. Three qualities replace quarreling: gentle toward all, able to teach, and patient. Verse 25 keeps correction in place but sets its tone: gentleness. The reason is hope for the opponent. God may give them repentance and knowledge of the truth. Verse 26 says they may yet escape the devil’s snare.

steps.title: Received Scripture equips conduct amid deceptive displays of religion
steps.text: Verse 13 says deceivers will grow worse. Verse 14 tells Timothy to stay with what he has learned. Verse 15 says the holy Scriptures can make him wise for salvation. Verse 16 lists four uses: teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. Verse 17 gives the purpose of all four. The person who belongs to God becomes complete. He is equipped “for every good work,” so the end of the list is action.

steps.title: Urgent teaching and ordinary needs stand together near the speaker's expected departure
steps.text: Verse 1 sets the charge before God and Christ the judge. Verse 2 gives five commands in a row. The first is to announce the word. The second is to be ready in season and out of season. Reprove, rebuke, and exhort follow, with patience and teaching. Verses 3–4 explain the urgency: hearers will turn from the truth to fables. Verse 6 adds another reason: Paul’s own departure is near.

chapterMaps.narrative: The letter is addressed from Paul to Timothy, his beloved child. Paul remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him. He recalls the faith of Timothy’s grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. Timothy is to stir up God’s gift, given through Paul’s hands. God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control, not fear. Timothy should not be ashamed of the Lord or of Paul the prisoner. All in Asia turned away from Paul. Onesiphorus was not ashamed of his chain and searched for him in Rome.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Rome, Ephesus, and Corinth as city points where each is named.
chapterMaps.narrative: Timothy is to be strong in grace and pass the teaching to faithful people. He should endure hardship like a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer. Paul suffers in chains, but God’s word is not chained. A trustworthy saying follows: if we died with him, we will live with him. Timothy should avoid word fights and empty talk. Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened. A great house has vessels for honor and for dishonor. The Lord’s servant must be gentle and correct opponents with patience.

chapterMaps.narrative: The letter warns that hard times will come in the last days. People will love themselves, money, and pleasure more than God. They will hold a form of godliness and deny its power. Such teachers resist the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. Timothy has followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, and sufferings at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. All who live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted. Timothy should continue in what he learned from childhood in the holy Scriptures. Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ, the judge of living and dead. Timothy is to announce the word and be ready at all times. A time will come when people gather teachers who please their ears. Paul says he is already being poured out. He has fought the good fight and kept the faith. He asks Timothy to come soon and bring Mark, a cloak, and the books. At his first defense no one stood with him, but the Lord did. He sends greetings and a blessing.
